Use the RLT package for Questions 1 and 2: RLT in R or rlt in Python. The node-size parameter is nmin in R and min_samples_leaf in Python; both stop splitting a node when it contains at most that many observations. The candidate-predictor parameter is mtry in both languages. Use ordinary random forests, with reinforcement turned off.

Question 1: Bias-variance trade-off simulation

Two important tuning parameters of random forests are node size and mtry. We have performed some preliminary analysis in class. The goal of this question is to perform a larger simulation study for these two tuning parameters.

Consider a regression model with five jointly normally distributed predictors. Each predictor has mean 0 and variance 1, and the correlation between any two different predictors is 0.3. The response is

Y=X1+X3+X5+ε,ε∼N(0,1), Y=X_1+X_3+X_5+\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,1),

where the noise is independent of the predictors. Thus the true regression function is f(𝒙)=x1+x3+x5f(\mathbf{x})=x_1+x_3+x_5.

  1. Set up a simulation study with 100 repetitions. Generate 200 test predictor vectors once and keep them fixed. In each repetition, generate 200 new training observations and use the same training data for all tuning settings. Fit 500-tree forests, drawing 200 observations with replacement for each tree. Make the following two comparisons:

    • Fix mtry at 3 and vary node size over 1,5,10,20,301,5,10,20,30.
    • Fix node size at 10 and vary mtry over 1,2,3,4,51,2,3,4,5.

    Leave all other fitting parameters at their defaults. Record the predictions at each test point across repetitions. For each setting, estimate the squared bias and variance at each test point, then average them over the 200 test points. Compare predictions with f(𝒙)f(\mathbf{x}) when estimating bias. Produce two figures, one for each tuning parameter, showing the averaged squared bias and variance. Set a random seed and report it.

  2. Discuss your results in terms of the bias-variance trade-off:

    • How does a large node size, such as 30, affect the fit in this example?
    • What are the benefits and drawbacks of using a large mtry value?
    • If each tree instead sampled 100 observations with replacement, would you expect the preferred node size to shift toward smaller or larger values? Explain your reasoning. You may use an additional simulation to help, but a particular pattern is not guaranteed.
set.seed(432)

nrep <- 100
node_sizes <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 30)
mtry_values <- 1:5

sigma <- matrix(0.3, nrow = 5, ncol = 5)
diag(sigma) <- 1

X_test <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = 200, mu = rep(0,5), Sigma = sigma)
f_test <- rowSums(X_test[, c(1, 3, 5)])

pred_node <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(200, nrep, length(node_sizes)))
pred_mtry <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(200, nrep, length(mtry_values)))

for (i in 1:nrep) {
   X_train <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = 200, mu = rep(0,5), Sigma = sigma)

   y_train <- rowSums(X_train[, c(1, 3, 5)]) + rnorm(200)

   for (j in seq_along(node_sizes)) {
      fit <- RLT::RLT(X_train, y_train, model = "regression", ntrees = 500, mtry = 3, 
         nmin = node_sizes[j], resample.prob = 1, resample.replace = TRUE,
         reinforcement = FALSE, seed = 432 + i)

      pred_node[, i, j] <- predict(fit, X_test)$Prediction
   }

   for (j in seq_along(mtry_values)) {
      fit <- RLT::RLT(X_train, y_train, model = "regression", ntrees = 500, 
         mtry = mtry_values[j], nmin = 10, resample.prob = 1, resample.replace = TRUE,
         reinforcement = FALSE, seed = 432 + i)

      pred_mtry[, i, j] <- predict(fit, X_test)$Prediction
   }
}

bias_node <- numeric(length(node_sizes))
var_node <- numeric(length(node_sizes))
bias_mtry <- numeric(length(mtry_values))
var_mtry <- numeric(length(mtry_values))

for (i in seq_along(node_sizes)) {
   predictions <- pred_node[, , i]
   bias_node[i] <- mean((rowMeans(predictions) - f_test)^2)
   var_node[i] <- mean(apply(predictions, 1, var))
}

for (i in seq_along(mtry_values)) {
   predictions <- pred_mtry[, , i]
   bias_mtry[i] <- mean((rowMeans(predictions) - f_test)^2)
   var_mtry[i] <- mean(apply(predictions, 1, var))
}

results_node <- data.frame(node_size = node_sizes, squared_bias = bias_node, variance = var_node)
results_mtry <- data.frame(mtry = mtry_values, squared_bias = bias_mtry, variance = var_mtry)

results_mtry

matplot(
  results_node$node_size,
  results_node[, c("squared_bias", "variance")],
  type = "b", pch = c(16, 17), lty = 1,
  col = c("blue", "red"),

  main = "Effect of mtry (node size = 10)"
)

  col = c("blue", "red"), pch = c(16, 17), lty = 1,
  bty = "n"
)

Large node size: Increasing node size from 1 to 30 increased squared bias from 0.1115 to 0.2172 and decreased variance from 0.1913 to 0.1515. A larger node-size threshold stops splitting earlier, producing less detailed trees. In this example, node size 30 sacrifices substantial accuracy in the average prediction for a relatively small reduction in variance.

Large mtry: Increasing mtry from 1 to 5 decreased squared bias from 0.3925 to 0.1003 but increased variance from 0.1098 to 0.2165. Considering more predictors at each split increases the chance of finding an informative split. However, trees can become more similar, reducing the variance-reduction benefit of averaging. Among the tested values, mtry = 3 had the smallest estimated squared bias plus variance.

Sampling 100 observations per tree: I would expect the preferred node size to shift toward smaller values. With fewer observations sampled per tree, the same node-size threshold stops splitting at a coarser level. A smaller threshold allows more splitting and may help preserve flexibility. However, smaller samples also make predictions less stable, so the best setting depends on the balance between bias and variance; the shift is not guaranteed.

Question 2: Tuning random forests for MNIST

Use mnist-first2000.csv.gz from the combined ZIP. It contains 2,000 MNIST observations, with the digit label Digit and 784 pixel values.

  • From the first 1,000 observations, keep digits 1, 6, and 7 as the training data. From the remaining 1,000 observations, keep the same digits as the test data.
  • Fit PCA to the training pixels, centering but not scaling them. Use the first 20 principal components as predictors, and project the test observations using the same training means and loadings.

Complete the following tasks using RLT classification forests with 1,000 trees. For each tree, draw a bootstrap sample of the same size as the training set.

  1. Fit a random forest with the default mtry and node-size settings. Report the out-of-bag (OOB) misclassification rate.

  2. Construct a grid of mtry and node-size values to tune the model. Select the setting using OOB misclassification rate. Report the OOB error for each setting and the selected values. Calculate and present the selected forest’s OOB permutation variable importance for the 20 principal components. Comment on your results.

  3. Apply the selected model to the test data and report the misclassification rate and confusion matrix. Use the test labels only for this final assessment.

set.seed(432)

mnist <- read.csv("data/mnist-first2000.csv.gz")

# Split by original row positions, then keep digits 1, 6, and 7
train <- mnist[1:1000, ]
test <- mnist[1001:2000, ]
train <- train[train$Digit %in% c(1, 6, 7), ]
test <- test[test$Digit %in% c(1, 6, 7), ]

y_train <- factor(train$Digit)
X_train <- train[, names(train) != "Digit"]
X_test <- test[, names(test) != "Digit"]

pca_fit <- prcomp(X_train, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
train_pc <- pca_fit$x[, 1:20]
test_pc <- predict(pca_fit, newdata = X_test)[, 1:20]

fit_default <- RLT::RLT(
  train_pc, y_train,
  model = "classification",
  ntrees = 1000,
  resample.prob = 1,
  resample.replace = TRUE,
  reinforcement = FALSE,
  seed = 432
)

oob_error <- mean(fit_default$Prediction != y_train)
oob_error
[1] 0.04281346
tuning_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20),
  nmin = c(1, 5, 10, 20)
)

tuning_grid$oob_error <- NA_real_
fits <- vector("list", nrow(tuning_grid))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(tuning_grid))) {

  fits[[i]] <- RLT::RLT(
   train_pc, y_train,
   model = "classification",
   ntrees = 1000,
   mtry = tuning_grid$mtry[i],
   nmin = tuning_grid$nmin[i],
   resample.prob = 1,
   resample.replace = TRUE,
   reinforcement = FALSE,
   importance = TRUE,
   seed = 432)

  tuning_grid$oob_error[i] <- mean(fits[[i]]$Prediction != y_train)
}

Using a seed of 432 and using 1,000 trees with the default settings of mtry = 10 and nmin = 5, the random forest had an OOB misclassification rate of approximately 4.28%. Each tree used a bootstrap sample of 327 training observations.

The selected forest used mtry = 1 and nmin = 1, achieving an OOB misclassification rate of approximately 1.53%, compared with 4.28% for the default forest. PC2 and PC1 had the largest permutation importance values, approximately 0.1295 and 0.0948, respectively. Shuffling these components caused the greatest deterioration in OOB prediction performance, indicating that they were particularly useful for distinguishing digits 1, 6, and 7. The remaining components had smaller positive importance values. The importance ranking does not exactly follow the PC order because PCA orders components by predictor variance, rather than usefulness for classification.

The selected random forest (mtry = 1, nmin = 1) achieved a test misclassification rate of approximately 1.58%, correctly classifying 312 of 317 observations. Two observations of digit 1 were classified as 7, and three observations of digit 7 were classified as 6. All 106 observations of digit 6 were classified correctly. The test error was close to the selected model’s OOB error of 1.53%.

Question 3: Planning a random-forest analysis skill

In earlier homework, some students wrote long skill files with detailed instructions, while others wrote short skills emphasizing their specific requirements or references. These approaches may perform differently depending on the AI and the task. A capable AI may already know standard ways to perform an analysis, so some instructions may be redundant, add little value, or sometimes make the analysis worse. It may be more useful to specify your personal choices for the analysis. An AI with more limited knowledge may benefit from detailed instructions that remind it of the steps to perform.

  1. Write one paragraph describing how you would write a skill that directs an AI to perform a random-forest analysis and produce a report for a future dataset. Discuss how you would balance standard analysis instructions with your personal preferences, considering the AI’s capabilities.

  2. Provide 10 instructions you would consider including in the skill, ordered from the most basic instructions to the more personal preferences. Your list may cover computation, tuning, tables, figures, interpretation, presentation, or other aspects of a random-forest report.

You only need to discuss how the skill should be written. You are not required to write a complete skill file or test it.

I would write a concise skill that emphasizes my preferences while including the essential steps needed for a reliable random-forest analysis. For a capable AI, I would briefly specify data preparation, tuning, and evaluation rather than explain every standard procedure. I would give more detailed instructions to an AI that needs additional guidance. My personal preferences would include explaining each step and its results in plain language, using reproducible results, and presenting clear tables and figures. This would make the skill useful without adding unnecessary instructions.

10 instructions I would consider including in the skill:

  1. Identify the response variable and determine whether the task is classification or regression.
  2. Check variable types, missing values, and whether any predictors reveal the response.
  3. Separate training and test data, fit preprocessing using training data only, and reserve the test set for final evaluation.
  4. Set and report random seeds, and record the package version and model settings.
  5. Tune mtry and node size using OOB error, reporting every setting evaluated and the selection rule.
  6. Evaluate the selected model on the test set using appropriate metrics, including a confusion matrix for classification.
  7. Present permutation variable importance and explain what it reveals about the fitted model without treating importance as evidence of causation.
  8. Use clearly labeled tables and figures that make model comparisons easy to understand.
  9. Preserve my existing code where it is correct and make only necessary changes. When changes are made, explain why they are needed and how they affect the analysis.
  10. Explain the analysis one step at a time in plain language, connecting the results to the bias-variance tradeoff of the analysis.
